opus-5.5.text:
Mathematics is unusually clean as a test. Most of what these models learn comes from imitating human text: predicting the next word of something a person already wrote. That makes it hard to tell whether a model is actually reasoning or just very good at reproducing what it has seen. With math, you can ask whether it can produce something nobody has written down yet.

Math also has a built-in referee. A proof is either correct or it isn't, and more and more you can check that mechanically with formal verification systems. So you don't depend on human judges deciding whether an answer *sounds* good, which is a weakness in many other domains. That matters for training too. Once you have a reliable verifier, you can let the system explore, generate attempts, check them, and learn from the ones that work. That loop can, in principle, take you past the level of the data you started with, the way self-play let game-playing systems surpass the best humans.

And it's a domain where going beyond people is plainly meaningful. If a system proves a theorem that mathematicians have been stuck on, or finds a new technique that other people then build on, that's hard to explain away as imitation. Nobody had the answer for it to copy.

Finally, the skills involved are general: searching enormous spaces of possibilities, forming abstractions, keeping a long chain of reasoning consistent, knowing when an idea is promising. If AI can really do that in mathematics, I think it's a strong signal that the same machinery can do original work in science and engineering. So math is both a benchmark and a proving ground for whether these systems can actually discover things.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can go beyond their starting data, but does not state that useful mathematical knowledge can be produced with roughly no external data.

r002.rationale: It argues that proving a theorem mathematicians were stuck on would be hard to explain as imitation because there was no answer for the system to copy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing about math is that it's one of the few places where you can actually check. If a model writes a poem or an essay, you're stuck with human judgment about whether it's good, and human judgment is exactly the thing we're trying to figure out whether we've exceeded. With a proof, you can verify it. Lean or some other proof assistant will tell you whether it holds, no opinions involved. So it's a clean signal.

And the second thing is that the space is genuinely open. There are conjectures that have been sitting there for decades, problems where the best mathematicians in the world have tried and not gotten there. If a model produces a correct proof of something nobody has proved before, there's no way to explain that as pattern-matching on the training set, because the answer wasn't in the training set. Nobody had it.

That's why I like it as a test. Most benchmarks, you're asking, can the model do what a smart person can do? And the honest answer is usually, well, it saw a lot of smart people doing that, so maybe. Math lets you ask the harder question, which is, can it do something nobody has done? And you get to find out without having to argue about it.

The other nice property is that it feeds back on itself. Math is the language of a lot of the rest of science, so if you get a system that's genuinely good at it, that isn't a parlor trick, that's a tool. I'm much more interested in that than in whether a model can pass a bar exam.

r001.rationale: It describes producing a correct proof of an unsolved conjecture whose answer was not in the training set, and says mathematical capability could become a useful tool for science.

r002.rationale: It argues that a correct proof of something nobody has proved before cannot be explained as pattern-matching on existing human work, directly challenging the idea that AI can only reproduce prior knowledge.

astra-6.text:
Well, mathematics is nice because you can check the answer. If a model comes up with a proof, you don’t have to decide whether it sounds like something a brilliant mathematician would say. You can actually check whether the proof is correct, potentially with a formal proof checker.

And there’s an enormous space of things that nobody has discovered yet. So you can ask a fairly concrete question: can the system prove something that wasn’t in its training data and that people didn’t already know how to prove?

That also gives you a way to train beyond imitation. You can have the system try things, get feedback on whether they work, and improve, rather than being limited to examples of what humans have done. Finding something interesting is another challenge—a correct theorem can still be completely uninteresting. But getting genuinely new, correct results would be a pretty compelling demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response describes discovering results absent from training data, but does not say this can produce useful knowledge from roughly no external data.

r002.rationale: It says genuinely new, correct results would demonstrate training beyond imitation, including proving something people did not already know how to prove.

sol-6.1.text: Well, with math, you can come up with something nobody’s seen before and actually check whether it’s right. If a model proves a conjecture that’s been open for a long time, and people can verify the proof, that’s pretty strong evidence that it’s doing more than reproducing an answer it saw in training. It’s still using ideas it learned from people, of course, but that’s what human mathematicians do too. The interesting question is whether it can put those ideas together to discover something new.

r001.rationale: The response says models use ideas learned from people; it does not claim mathematical discovery can produce useful knowledge with roughly no external data.

r002.rationale: It says a verifiable proof of a long-open conjecture would show the model is doing more than reproducing training answers, and frames the goal as discovering something new.
